title: The Math You Need: Powers, Logarithms and Sums
oneLiner: Three pieces of school math that explain most of computing's numbers: powers of two, logarithms as "how many halvings", and the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n.
keyTakeaway: Powers of two count what bits can hold: n bits give 2^n different values, and 2^10 is about a thousand. A logarithm runs that backwards: log2(n) is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, which is why halving algorithms such as binary search stay fast on huge inputs. And 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2, roughly n^2 / 2, which is why a loop inside a loop is O(n^2).
explanation:
You don't need much math to program, but a few ideas come up constantly, especially once you start asking how fast code is (Big O Notation, in Data Structures & Algorithms). This lesson covers them with sliders instead of proofs.

An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself: 2^3 means 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, and 10^6 is a million. Powers of two matter because computers count in bits, and each extra bit doubles how many values you can represent: 1 bit has 2 values, 8 bits (a byte) have 2^8 = 256, and 32 bits have about 4.3 billion. A handy coincidence: 2^10 = 1,024, close to a thousand, so 2^20 is about a million and 2^30 about a billion. That's why memory sizes come in KB, MB and GB steps of roughly 1,000.

A logarithm is an exponent run backwards. log2(8) = 3 because 2^3 = 8: it answers "2 to the what gives me this number?" The practical way to think about it: log2(n) is how many times you can cut n in half before you get down to 1. Halving is incredibly effective. A million halves to 1 in about 20 steps, and a billion in about 30, so an algorithm that throws away half the remaining work each step (O(log n)) barely notices the input growing. Doubling and halving are mirror images: exponential growth (2^n) explodes, logarithmic growth (log n) almost stands still.

Finally, sums. Adding 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n gives n(n + 1) / 2: pair the first and last numbers (1 + n), the second and second-to-last (2 + (n - 1)), and every pair adds to the same n + 1. This sum appears whenever an inner loop runs a little longer each time round an outer loop, for example comparing each item with every item before it. For large n it is about n^2 / 2, so in Big O terms it's O(n^2). Try the three widgets below, then the growth table at the end shows why n^2, 2^n and n! (n factorial, 1 x 2 x ... x n) quickly become impossible.
